Das Wort, jetzt whittle ‘weisser Mantel, Laken, Shawl’, übersetzt sagum, pallium. [Die Bed. Messer, die jetzt ein anderes Wort whittle hat, kommt Agsächs. nicht vor.] Vgl. Gl Kleidung 5; Abgabe 15C. Festländischen Kleiderzins s. Grimm DRA 378; von hörigen Hufen liefern die Frauen Gewebe an Karls d. Gr. Hof; Klumker Fries. Tuchhandel in Jahrb. Gesell. Emden 13 (1899) 39. [In der von Kemble Saxons I 318 für ‘rent and vestment’ zitierten Urk. Bi 582 lies nicht rift, sondern scrift]. Aus späterem Englischen MA. kennen ‘rents in linen, cloth’ Vinogradoff Growth 329, Neilson Customary rents 191

The word, now whittle ‘white cloak, sheet, shawl’, translates sagum, pallium. [The meaning ‘knife’, now borne by a different word whittle, does not occur in Anglo-Saxon.] Cf. Gl Kleidung 5; Abgabe 15C. For rent paid in clothing on the Continent see Grimm DRA 378; from servile hides the women deliver woven cloth to the court of Charles the Great; Klumker Fries. Tuchhandel in Jahrb. Gesell. Emden 13 (1899) 39. [In the charter Bi 582, cited by Kemble Saxons I 318 for ‘rent and vestment’, read not rift but scrift]. ‘Rents in linen, cloth’ from the later English Middle Ages are noted by Vinogradoff Growth 329, Neilson Customary rents 191
Nicht ‘für’ sondern ab, de, ex. So übersetzt offrian æt ælcum hiwisce an lamb: tollat unusquisque agnum per familias et domos suas; Ælfric Homil. 310 = Exod. 12, 3
Not ‘for’ but ab, de, ex. Thus offrian æt ælcum hiwisce an lamb translates tollat unusquisque agnum per familias et domos suas; Ælfric Homil. 310 = Exod. 12, 3

Vgl. Gl Hufe 1a. 5. 16a; jedenfalls nicht von jedem Kötter- oder Arbeiterhäuschen. Diese Abgabe — nur eine neben anderen Naturalien; s. 70, 1 — ist für 692 nicht zu klein für die ganze Hufe, da ja damals Mutterschaf mit Lamm nur 5 Pf. galt, und Steuer von 24 Pf. im ganzen auf 1 Hufe um 1000 und 1100 arg drückte. Dass in Urk. Bi 594 hiwisc das später gewöhnliche Bauernzinsgut von nur ¹/₄ Hufe bedeuten könne, leugnet Maitland Domesday 361

Cf. Gl Hufe 1a. 5. 16a; at any rate not from every cottar’s or labourer’s cottage. This due — only one among other payments in kind; see 70, 1 — is not too small for the whole hide in 692, since at that time a ewe with lamb was valued at only 5 pence, and a tax of 24 pence in all on 1 hide around 1000 and 1100 was a heavy burden. That in the charter Bi 594 hiwisc could mean the later usual peasant’s rent-holding of only ¹/₄ hide is denied by Maitland Domesday 361
‘Fünf’ Q, vielleicht weil 5 Pfennig (s. d. Gl 3; Murray New Engl. dict. VII 647 beanstandet dieses Wortes wegen die Authentizität Ines nicht) 1 Schilling machen
‘Five’ Q, perhaps because 5 pence (see that word in Gl 3; Murray New Engl. dict. VII 647 does not question Ine’s authenticity on account of this word) make 1 shilling

note.seg: syx penega wurð. B. peninga wyrð. H.
For ‘rents in linen, cloth’ in later times see Vinogradoff, The Growth of the Manor, p. 329; Neilson, Customary Rents, p. 191.

hiwisc is apparently used in the Northleoda Laga, cap. 7, for hid, the original meaning of which was the portion of land appertaining to a household (Lat. familia). It is very likely that hiwisc has the same meaning here, i.e. as Liebermann suggests, the tax would not be paid by the cottager who held little or no land.

note.label: household
note.seg: Or perhaps hiwisc means here, as sometimes elsewhere, a hide of land. I am uncertain whether the meaning is that a “blanket” was paid from each household with at least one hide of land, or else one had to be rendered for every hide.
